parts.title: Booking a first-aid course
parts.context: A man books a first-aid course required by his employer.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a training centre to book a first-aid course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: You will see that there is an example that has been done for you. On this occasion only, the conversation relating to this will be played first.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Safe Hands Training, Joanne speaking.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Hello. I'd like to book a place on your first-aid course, please. My employer requires everyone on site to have the certificate.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Of course. I'll take some details first.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: The course is needed for work, so 'work' has been written in the space. Now we shall begin. You should answer the questions as you listen, because you will not hear the recording a second time. Listen carefully and answer questions 1 to 5.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Could I have your name, please?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Raj Kapoor. That's K-A-P-O-O-R.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Thank you, Mr Kapoor. What is your job?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: I'm a plumber. I work on building sites, so first aid is quite important.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: I can see why. Which date would suit you?

script.speaker: raj
script.text: The twelfth of March, if you have a place.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: We do. The course lasts six hours, so it's a full day.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: That's fine. What time does it start?

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Registration is at half past eight, but the training itself starts at nine, so please be on time.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 6 to 10.

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: The fee is seventy-five pounds, and that includes the certificate and a small first-aid manual.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: That's good value. Where is the course held?

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: At the Community Centre, on Mill Road. It's next to the swimming pool, and there's free parking at the back.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Is there a place to buy lunch nearby?

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: There's a café across the road, but most people bring a packed lunch, because the break is quite short.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: And what should I wear?

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Loose clothes that you can move in easily, because you'll be kneeling on the floor and practising on the dummies.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: How long does the certificate last?

script.speaker: joanne
script.text: Three years. After that, you'll need a refresher course, and we'll remind you by email.

script.speaker: raj
script.text: Excellent. Can I pay by card now?

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 1. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A first-aid course
parts.context: An instructor welcomes a group to a first-aid course.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 2. You will hear an instructor welcoming a group to a first-aid course. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 11 to 15.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the course. I'm Tony Dunn, and I'll be your instructor today. There are twelve of you, which is a good number, because everyone will get plenty of practice.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Let's start with the most important rule of first aid. Before you do anything else, check that the area is safe, for you, for the casualty and for anyone else. It's no use becoming a second casualty.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Next, we'll learn CPR, which is used when somebody's heart has stopped. You push down firmly on the middle of the chest at a rate of about a hundred times a minute, and that's quicker than most people expect.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: After lunch, we'll look at burns. For a serious burn, the best treatment is to cool it under cool running water for at least twenty minutes. Please don't use ice, and never put butter on a burn, which is an old myth that makes things worse.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: You'll be practising on dummies, which are in the next room, so you don't have to worry about hurting anyone. Nobody has to practise on each other.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the talk, you have some time to look at questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 16 to 20.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Let me say something about heart attacks. The best known symptom is pain in the chest, a feeling of heaviness, but also pain which spreads to the arm, the neck or the jaw. People often think they're having indigestion, so they wait too long, and that is dangerous. If you're in doubt, call the emergency number.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: What about an unconscious person who is still breathing? You should put them in the recovery position, on their side, with the head tilted back, so that they can breathe and nothing blocks their throat. Don't give them anything to drink.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: At the end of the day, there's a practical test. You'll show us that you can do CPR, and put somebody in the recovery position. There's no written exam, and in nearly every course, everyone passes.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Your certificate will be sent to you by email within a week, and if you need a paper copy, you can ask the office.

script.speaker: dunn
script.text: Right, shall we begin? Please turn off your phones, unless you need to keep one on for work.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 2. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: A student satisfaction survey
parts.context: Two statistics students discuss sampling methods for their survey.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 3. You will hear two statistics students, Tilda and Ahmed, discussing a student satisfaction survey. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 21 to 25.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: Ahmed, shall we go through the survey report? I'll start with the sample. We sent the questionnaire to six hundred students, didn't we?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: Yes, six hundred, but only two hundred and fifty replied, so our sample is two hundred and fifty.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: That's a response rate of about forty percent. Not wonderful, but not terrible for an online survey.

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: Not wonderful, no. And the other problem was with the questions. Several respondents said that question seven was confusing, so we can't use those answers.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: What about the margin of error? I calculated it as plus or minus six percent.

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: I'd say that's acceptable for a student project. A professional survey would want it smaller, but we'd need a much bigger sample for that.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: Agreed. What shall we say in the conclusion?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: That a larger sample would give more reliable results, and that the university should repeat the survey next year, using a shorter questionnaire.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen and answer questions 26 to 30.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: In the methodology, we should explain the sampling methods we considered. Simple random sampling first.

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: It's the textbook method, but it needs a complete list of the whole population, and the university couldn't give us one.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: Stratified sampling?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: That ensures that each group is represented, for example each year and each faculty, so it's more accurate when the groups differ.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: Convenience sampling?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: That's the easiest, just asking whoever is nearby, but it's biased, so it's not suitable for conclusions about all students.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: Cluster sampling?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: It's cheap when the population is spread over many places, because you survey whole groups, like entire classes, instead of individuals.

script.speaker: tilda
script.text: And quota sampling?

script.speaker: ahmed
script.text: That's the method we actually used, in the end, taking a fixed number from each faculty, so we'll describe it in detail.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 3. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

parts.title: Lecture: the history of money
parts.context: A lecture on money from barter to digital currencies.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about the history of money. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: Now listen carefully and answer questions 31 to 40.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Good morning. Money is so familiar that we rarely ask where it came from. Today I'd like to trace its history, from the earliest exchanges to the digital payments of today.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Before money, people used barter, which means exchanging one good directly for another. But barter has a big problem. It only works if each person wants what the other has. If I have fish and want a pair of shoes, I must find a shoemaker who wants fish.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: So people began to use items that everyone accepted. Early forms of money included shells, salt and cattle. These were useful, but not ideal, because cattle are difficult to carry, and shells can be collected by anyone.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The first coins were made in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, about six hundred years before Christ. They were small pieces of metal, an alloy of gold and silver, stamped with a mark which guaranteed their value.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In China, around the tenth century, merchants faced a different problem. Their coins were so heavy that a large purchase needed a cart. So paper money appeared, which was far more convenient to carry.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: Europe was slower. The first European banknotes were issued in Sweden in sixteen sixty-one. Banknotes were originally promises to pay the holder a certain amount of gold, and that is why banks kept gold in their vaults.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: In the nineteen fifties, the first credit card was introduced, allowing people to buy now and pay later. Today most money exists only as numbers on a computer, and cash is used less each year.

script.speaker: lecturer
script.text: The latest development is digital currencies. Some of them use a system called blockchain, in which a record of every transaction is shared across thousands of computers, with no central bank. Whether they will last is still an open question. Next week we'll look at banking.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of Part 4. You now have half a minute to check your answers.

script.speaker: narrator
script.text: That is the end of the Listening test.
